title: Why the Sleep Experiment Went Wrong
context: A psychology tutor goes through a pilot study with the two students who ran it, and takes apart the way it was designed.

script.speaker: Dr Vance
script.text: Right, let's look at your pilot. You ran it over three weeks, is that right?

script.speaker: Aisha
script.text: Three weeks, yes. Twenty-two participants in the end.

script.speaker: Ewan
script.text: Twenty-four signed up, though. Two of them dropped out halfway.

script.speaker: Aisha
script.text: Sorry, yes — twenty-four signed up, twenty-two finished. Twenty-two is the number that matters.

script.speaker: Dr Vance
script.text: It is. And your finding was that the group who napped remembered more words. How much more?

script.speaker: Ewan
script.text: About eleven per cent more, on average.

script.speaker: Dr Vance
script.text: Which sounds impressive until you look at the spread. What was your standard deviation?

script.speaker: Aisha
script.text: It was... quite large. Larger than the difference between the groups, actually.

script.speaker: Dr Vance
script.text: Larger than the difference. So what does that tell you?

script.speaker: Ewan
script.text: That the result could easily just be noise.

script.speaker: Dr Vance
script.text: It could. It might not be — but with twenty-two people you can't tell, and that's the honest position to take. Now, before we come back to the numbers, there's something else I want you to notice. How did people end up in the nap group?

script.speaker: Aisha
script.text: They chose. We asked who was willing to nap and who'd rather stay awake.

script.speaker: Dr Vance
script.text: Right.

script.speaker: Ewan
script.text: Ah.

script.speaker: Aisha
script.text: What?

script.speaker: Ewan
script.text: The people who volunteered to nap are... they're different people to begin with. They're people who can nap.

script.speaker: Dr Vance
script.text: Go on.

script.speaker: Ewan
script.text: And in our own questionnaire — I've only just remembered this — the nap group reported drinking less coffee. Much less. We wrote it down and then never thought about it again.

script.speaker: Dr Vance
script.text: So you have two groups that differ in more than one way, and a result you would like to attribute to just one of those ways. That is the whole problem in a single sentence. What is it called?

script.speaker: Aisha
script.text: It's a confounding variable.

script.speaker: Dr Vance
script.text: It is. And the fix is not cleverer statistics, it's the design. You allocate people at random, and you don't let them pick.

script.speaker: Aisha
script.text: Some of them won't be able to nap, though.

script.speaker: Dr Vance
script.text: Then they lie down in a dark room for forty minutes and you record whether they actually slept. That is data, not a failure. What you must not do is let the participant choose the condition.

script.speaker: Ewan
script.text: Can I ask about the ethics side? Our approval came through in week two, and we'd already run four people by then.

script.speaker: Dr Vance
script.text: Then those four don't exist. You take them out and you say so in the write-up. I would far rather read a study that reports twenty-two people and one honest paragraph about four excluded ones, than a study that quietly reports twenty-six.

script.speaker: Aisha
script.text: That does weaken the result, though.

script.speaker: Dr Vance
script.text: It weakens the number. It strengthens the paper. Those are not the same thing.

script.speaker: Ewan
script.text: What about the memory test itself? We used a list of forty words.

script.speaker: Dr Vance
script.text: How were they chosen?

script.speaker: Ewan
script.text: We picked them ourselves.

script.speaker: Dr Vance
script.text: On what basis?

script.speaker: Ewan
script.text: Um. We thought they seemed... ordinary.

script.speaker: Dr Vance
script.text: There are published word lists, matched for frequency and length, precisely so that the phrase "seemed ordinary" doesn't have to do that work for you. Use one. That is the easiest of all the changes on this list, and it costs you nothing at all.

script.speaker: Aisha
script.text: So for the main study — random allocation, a standard word list, and ethics approval before anybody walks through the door.

script.speaker: Dr Vance
script.text: And more people. How many can you realistically recruit next term?

script.speaker: Aisha
script.text: Sixty? Maybe seventy if we can use the second-year pool as well.

script.speaker: Dr Vance
script.text: Aim for sixty and be pleased if you get seventy. Now — one thing you did do well, and I don't want it lost in all of this. Your timing was identical for every participant. Same hour of the day, same interval between learning and testing, to the minute. That is genuinely careful work and most pilots don't manage it.

script.speaker: Ewan
script.text: That was Aisha's doing.

script.speaker: Aisha
script.text: It was both of us.

script.speaker: Dr Vance
script.text: Well, keep doing it. Right — Ewan, find me two candidate word lists by Friday. Aisha, write the ethics application this week, not next week. And both of you, one page on how you intend to randomise.

script.speaker: Aisha
script.text: One page each, or one page between us?

script.speaker: Dr Vance
script.text: Between you. If you can't agree on it now, you certainly won't agree on it in February.

questions.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.

questions.question: How many participants completed the pilot study?
questions.explanation: Twenty-four signed up but two dropped out, and Aisha corrects herself: "twenty-four signed up, twenty-two finished. Twenty-two is the number that matters."

questions.question: What does Aisha say about the standard deviation?
options: it was smaller than the difference between the groups
it was larger than the difference between the groups
questions.explanation: She says it was "quite large. Larger than the difference between the groups," which is why Ewan concludes the result could be noise.

questions.question: What was wrong with the way participants were put into groups?
options: the participants chose their own group
the groups were of very different sizes
the groups were decided by age
questions.explanation: Aisha explains, "They chose. We asked who was willing to nap." Dr Vance's rule is: "You allocate people at random, and you don't let them pick."

questions.question: What does Dr Vance tell the students to do about the four people tested before ethics approval?
options: include them but add a note
test the same four people again
questions.explanation: "Those four don't exist. You take them out and you say so in the write-up." He prefers an honest paragraph to a quiet total of twenty-six.

questions.question: What does Dr Vance praise about the pilot study?
questions.explanation: "Your timing was identical for every participant. Same hour of the day, same interval between learning and testing, to the minute."

questions.instruction: Complete the sentences below. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.

questions.sentence: The questionnaire showed that the nap group drank less ___
questions.explanation: Ewan suddenly remembers it: "the nap group reported drinking less coffee. Much less. We wrote it down and then never thought about it again."

questions.sentence: Two groups that differ in more than one way create a ___ variable
questions.explanation: Aisha supplies the term when Dr Vance asks what the problem is called: "It's a confounding variable."

questions.sentence: Participants who cannot sleep should lie in a dark room for ___ minutes
questions.explanation: "Then they lie down in a dark room for forty minutes and you record whether they actually slept. That is data, not a failure."

questions.sentence: Published word lists are matched for length and ___
questions.explanation: Dr Vance recommends "published word lists, matched for frequency and length," instead of words the students judged to be ordinary.

questions.sentence: For the main study the students should aim to recruit ___ participants
questions.explanation: "Aim for sixty and be pleased if you get seventy." Seventy is the hoped-for figure, not the target they should plan around.
